MICROGRID: POWER MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS


1. Introduction



1.1 Overview


As a passionate advocate for clean energy, I embarked on a personal project to create a power management system in microgrid. This system is designed to ensure that when there is shortage of power, the systems will interupt the delivery of electricity of certain non-essential (non-critcal loads) to maintain the integrity of electric grid and preserve power for critical loads, such as Life-saving Hospitals, Emergency Services, Military installations and Financial Institutions.



1.2 Project Goals

To make an optimized load shedding process to balance the supply and demand and maintain the stability of the electrical grid.


2. Why Load Shedding?

Load shedding is a crucial practice employed by utility companies to maintain the stability of electrical grids. This controlled reduction of power consumption becomes necessary during periods of high demand or unexpected disturbances to prevent grid instability, equipment damage, and the risk of widespread blackouts. By strategically shedding non-essential loads, load shedding ensures that the electrical system operates within safe parameters, protecting critical infrastructure, and prioritizing essential and critical loads. It is a proactive measure that safeguards against potential failures, supporting the reliability and resilience of the power grid in the face of challenges.


3. System Components And How It Works



3.1 ESP32 DevKit


The microcontroller serves as the central processing unit, gathering data from sensors, performing calculations, make decision to manage loads and controlling the relay switch.



3.2 Solar Panel


This acts as one of the renewable energy sources that is used to power up the load.



3.3 Wind Generator


Wind generator will provide extra power to power up the load alongside with solar panel. Since the microgrid is not grid-connected, the system relies heavily on both of these renewable energy sources.



3.4 Energy Storage (Battery)


This component is essential as it is being used to storage excess energy produced by both Solar Panel and Wind Generator. Since solar panel does not produce much power at night and Wind generator does not produce power when there is no wind, the excess energy stored from the energy storge (battery) will be used to power up the loads.



3.5 Three Phase Rectifier


The wind generator generates 3 phase AC and the energy storage (battery) stores energy in DC. This component will convert AC power from the generator to DC Power and able to store its energy in the battery.



3.6 Buck Converter


Although we already rectifed the power from wind generator from AC to DC, it is important to make sure the DC voltage of the wind generator matches voltage the energy storage (battery). In this case, the battery is rated 3.7V and the wind generator produces higher voltage. Buck converter is used to step down the DC Voltage of the wind generator to matches the battery voltage.



3.7 MPPT Solar Charger


MPPT checks output of PV module, compares it to battery voltage then fixes what is the best power that PV module can produce to charge the battery and converts it to the best voltage to get maximum current into battery. It can also supply power to loads, which is connected directly to the battery.



3.8 Boost Converter


The output from the MPPT Solar Charger is rated 3.7V DC while the load are rated 12V AC. Boost Converter is used to boost voltage from 3.7V to 12V DC.



3.9 Inverter


The inverter will convert the 12V DC from boost converter to 12V AC to supply for the loads



3.10 Relay Switch


Act as switches that open and close the circuits by receiving electrical signals from outside sources. In this case ESP32



3.11 Loads (Light Bulbs)


I use 3 bulbs to represent 3 different types of loads, which is Critical Load, Industrial Load and Domestic Load



3.12 Battery Level Gauge


To monitor and determine the State of Charge (SOC) of the battery and then send the signal to the ESP32.



3.13 AWG16 Wire


Jumper wire is not suitable for this project as the current will be higher than 2A. This type of wire is rated to conduct maximum current of 10A .

9. Software and Libraries

Highlight code with copy button 
                          
                            #define BLYNK_TEMPLATE_ID "TMPL61aPbFDQa"
                            #define BLYNK_TEMPLATE_NAME "Engineering Team project"
                            #define BLYNK_AUTH_TOKEN "xclloEt2T11ZkKrAYy9mPHydh1BgrmMo"
                            
                            #include <Ticker.h>
                            #include <DFRobot_MAX17043.h>
                            #include <BlynkSimpleEsp32.h>

                            DFRobot_MAX17043 FuelGauge;  // Declare FuelGauge globally

                            unsigned long simulatedTime = 0;
                            const unsigned long timeStep = 5000;  // 5 seconds

                            #define RELAY1_PIN 32  // Replace with the actual pin connected to relay 1
                            #define RELAY2_PIN 33  // Replace with the actual pin connected to relay 2

                            //========================= Variables for wifi server setup =============================
                            const char *ssid = "Durrani";
                            const char *password = "87654321";
                            const char *blynkAuth = "xclloEt2T11ZkKrAYy9mPHydh1BgrmMo";

                            Ticker timer;

                            float prevBatteryPercentage = 0.0;
                            unsigned long prevUpdateTime = 0;
                            float batteryChangeRate = 0.0;

                            void setup() {
                              Serial.begin(115200);
                              Serial.println("Simulation, Battery Gauge, and Relay Control started.");

                              WiFi.begin(ssid, password);
                              while (WiFi.status() != WL_CONNECTED) {
                                delay(500);
                                Serial.print(".");
                              }
                              Serial.println("\nConnected to Wi-Fi");
                              Blynk.begin(blynkAuth, ssid, password);

                              FuelGauge.begin();

                              // Initialize relay pins as OUTPUT
                              pinMode(RELAY1_PIN, OUTPUT);
                              pinMode(RELAY2_PIN, OUTPUT);

                              // Turn off relays initially
                              digitalWrite(RELAY1_PIN, HIGH);
                              digitalWrite(RELAY2_PIN, HIGH);

                              timer.attach_ms(timeStep, updateSimulatedTime);
                            }

                            void loop() {
                              // Your simulation logic here

                              // Read battery gauge
                              float batteryPercentage = FuelGauge.readPercentage()-59;
                              float batteryVoltage = FuelGauge.readVoltage()/1000;

                              // Calculate the rate of change
                              unsigned long currentTime = millis();
                              unsigned long elapsedTime = currentTime - prevUpdateTime;

                              if (elapsedTime > 0) {
                                batteryChangeRate = (batteryPercentage - prevBatteryPercentage) / (elapsedTime / 1000.0);
                              }

                              // Update previous values for the next iteration
                              prevBatteryPercentage = batteryPercentage;
                              prevUpdateTime = currentTime;

                              // Relay control based on battery percentage and time
                              controlRelays(batteryPercentage, simulatedTime);

                              // Display battery gauge information
                              Serial.println("Battery Gauge Information:");
                              Serial.printf("  Battery percentage: %.2f%%\n", batteryPercentage);
                              Serial.printf("  Battery voltage: %.2fV\n", batteryVoltage);
                              Serial.printf("  Battery change rate: %.2f%%/s\n", batteryChangeRate);

                              delay(1000);  // Add a delay for better readability in the Serial Monitor
                            }

                            void updateSimulatedTime() {
                              simulatedTime = (simulatedTime + 1) % 24;

                              unsigned long twelveHourFormat = simulatedTime % 12;
                              if (twelveHourFormat == 0) {
                                twelveHourFormat = 12;
                              }

                              const char* amPmIndicator = (simulatedTime < 12) ? "AM" : "PM";

                              Serial.printf("Current Simulated Time: %02lu:00 %s\n", twelveHourFormat, amPmIndicator);
                            }

                            void controlRelays(float batteryPercentage, unsigned long currentTime) {
                              if (batteryPercentage > 50) {
                                // Battery higher than 50%, turn off both relays
                                digitalWrite(RELAY1_PIN, HIGH);
                                digitalWrite(RELAY2_PIN, HIGH);
                              } else if (batteryPercentage >= 26 && batteryPercentage <= 50) {
                                // Battery between 26% and 50%
                                // Turn on relay 1 if it's not between 9 AM and 5 PM, otherwise, turn on relay 2
                                if (currentTime < 9 || currentTime >= 17) {
                                  digitalWrite(RELAY1_PIN, LOW);
                                  digitalWrite(RELAY2_PIN, HIGH);
                                  Blynk.logEvent("Shedding Industrial Load");
                                } else {
                                  digitalWrite(RELAY1_PIN, HIGH);
                                  digitalWrite(RELAY2_PIN, LOW);
                                  Blynk.logEvent("Shedding Residential Load");
                                }
                              } else {
                                // Battery 25% and below, turn on both relays
                                digitalWrite(RELAY1_PIN, LOW);
                                digitalWrite(RELAY2_PIN, LOW);
                                Blynk.logEvent("Maintenance needed: Power ratio is out of range!");
                              }
                              Blynk.run();
                              Blynk.virtualWrite(V0, batteryPercentage);
                              Blynk.virtualWrite(V1, simulatedTime);
                              Blynk.virtualWrite(V2, batteryChangeRate);
                            }
